sources.title: Chapter 10 - Principles of Pipelining (Basic Computer Architecture)
sources.channel: IIT Delhi, Prof. Smruti R. Sarangi (freely distributed book chapter)
sources.note: the whole 92-page chapter was read: the pipeline idea and its performance, the five stages, pipeline registers, data/control/structural hazards, software solutions, interlocks and bubbles, forwarding paths and conditions, interrupts, the performance equation, branch prediction, multiple issue and out-of-order execution

sourceLine: The interlock and its data-lock unit, the branch-lock unit, and bubbles inserted by clearing control signals: Sarangi chapter 10, sections 10.6.1 to 10.6.3 (English, read in full). The stall counts of 2, 0 and 1 for the three RAW situations: DSWallah Learn 'Pipeline Hazards & Stalls', romanised Hindi, translated (read in part).
title: Stalls, Interlocks and Bubbles: Counting the Cycles
unit: Instruction Pipelining: Hazards, Stalls and Fixes
quickIdea: When the value cannot arrive in time, the interlock freezes the front of the pipeline and inserts a bubble: the dependent instruction repeats a stage while everything behind it waits. A bubble costs one cycle of throughput and shows in the diagram as an empty column.
remember: The data-lock unit detects a RAW pair whose distance is smaller than the available forwarding allows, and holds the PC and the front-end registers for the cycles needed.
Load-use in the 5-stage pipeline costs exactly 1 bubble; a RAW pair with no forwarding path costs 2.
A bubble is made by clearing the control signals of the stage it occupies, so it changes no architectural state.
When every stall is at the front, total cycles = (k + n - 1) + total stall cycles.
When a stage is variable-length instead, the stage never idles: total cycles = (fill) + (sum of the stage's occupancies) + (drain), which is why (k + n - 1) alone fails on GATE CSE 2018 Q.50.

example.prompt: A 5-stage RISC pipeline has IF, ID, OF, PO, WB, where IF, ID, OF and WB take 1 cycle each and PO takes 3 cycles for 40 instructions, 2 for 35 and 1 for the remaining 25. With no data or control hazards, how many cycles does the sequence of 100 instructions need?
example.work: The PO unit is the bottleneck and never idles once it starts. Its total occupancy is 40x3 + 35x2 + 25x1 = 120 + 70 + 25 = 215 cycles. Before the first instruction reaches PO, IF, ID and OF take 3 cycles; after the last leaves PO, WB takes 1. Total = 3 + 215 + 1 = 219. Equivalently (5 + 100 - 1) + (40x2 + 35x1) = 104 + 115 = 219.
example.answer: 219 cycles, the accepted answer of GATE CSE 2018 Q.50.

gateAngle: There are two distinct counting questions and they must not be mixed. Stall-at-the-front questions add bubbles to (k + n - 1); variable-stage questions add the stage's extra occupancy, 115 here, to the same base. GATE CSE 2018 Q.50 is the second kind, and 2026 Set 1 Q.60 counts the same extra occupancy as 'structural hazard stalls'.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: In the 2018 Q.50 sequence, what changes if the 40 three-cycle instructions are made one cycle each by a pipelined PO unit?
variations.why: It separates the two counting methods by removing the bottleneck instead of adding stalls.
variations.answer: PO occupancy becomes 100, so the total is 3 + 100 + 1 = 104, exactly (k + n - 1). The 115 extra cycles were the price of the multi-cycle unit, not of any dependence in the program.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does inserting a bubble not change the result of the program?
variations.why: It answers the natural worry that a stall is a wasted instruction rather than a delayed one.
variations.answer: Because a bubble has its control signals cleared, so it writes no register, touches no memory and raises no exception. It occupies a stage for a cycle and then disappears; the dependent instruction executes again in the next cycle and reads the value that has by then arrived.

trap.what: Averaging the variable stage and then using (k + n - 1).
trap.why: The average occupancy hides the fact that the stage is busy continuously; the correct total is the sum of occupancies plus fill and drain, and the average-based formula gives 104 + something arbitrary.
trap.counterexample: 2018 Q.50 with average PO 2.15 cycles: the naive route gives 6.15 + 99 x 2.15 = 219 only if done carefully, and most shortcuts give 104 or 215 instead of the accepted 219.

check.question: A 5-stage pipeline runs 20 instructions with 3 load-use bubbles. How many cycles does it take?
check.explanation: The base pipeline is k + n - 1 = 24; each bubble is one more column, so the stalls are added, not multiplied.
